claims.text: In single-phase FCC high-entropy alloys, toughness retention is governed by localized chemical and lattice heterogeneities that produce a broad, low but spatially variable stacking-fault-energy distribution.
Heterogeneous stacking-fault energy enables nano-twinning, multiple kinks or jogs, and bidirectional cross-slip.
These unconventional dislocation processes bridge cracks and delay catastrophic failure.
A minor additive that raises average stacking-fault energy and reduces its spatial variability will suppress the beneficial dislocation mechanisms and reduce toughness.
A homogeneous, single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy naturally has low and heterogeneous local stacking-fault energy because of random elemental mixing.
An approximately 1–2 atomic percent addition of an element known to increase average stacking-fault energy can be used to modify the local chemical environment.
Dislocation slip and twinning remain active from room temperature to intermediate elevated temperatures as high as about 800 °C in the proposed alloys.
Local stacking-fault-energy variation arises from chemical heterogeneity, lattice strain, and local short-range order.
Low average stacking-fault energy with possible local variation modulates full- and partial-dislocation behavior.
Heterogeneous lattice strain causes multiple dislocation kinks or jogs and bidirectional cross-slip.
Alloy chemistry is a primary factor governing the emergence of twinning in metastable multicomponent alloys.
Short-range order creates chemical heterogeneity and can substantially alter dislocation-slip behavior.
Unconventional dislocation pathways provide intrinsic crack bridging and delay crack initiation.
The controlled additive will produce a more uniform stacking-fault-energy distribution as well as a higher average stacking-fault energy.
Relative to the baseline, the modified alloy will show fewer nanotwins, altered dislocation configurations, and lower fracture toughness.
The baseline random solid solution has a broad local stacking-fault-energy distribution that enables several dislocation-mediated toughening processes.
The proposed behavior is limited to stable, single-phase FCC high-entropy alloys and may fail after segregation or precipitation or in BCC and HCP alloys where other deformation mechanisms dominate.
The cited evidence establishes a correlation between stacking-fault-energy heterogeneity and activation of multiple dislocation mechanisms.
Failure to observe statistically significant reductions in unconventional dislocation features or any measurable toughness decrease in the modified samples would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The initial state and baseline are described as random elemental mixing or a random solid solution, while local short-range order is invoked as a governing source of chemical heterogeneity. Short-range order is non-random, so the hypothesis needs to distinguish random compositional fluctuations from genuine non-random ordering.
